design_detail: National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) statistical report, National Vital Statistics Reports vol. 75, no. 1 (5 March 2026, pp. 1 to 13), updating the 2011 to 2016 report in the same series. Data: the 2017 to 2023 National Vital Statistics System (NVSS) mortality files for US residents who died in the United States, linked to the literal text of death certificates, retrieved from NCHS's live database on 6 April 2025. A death enters the overdose count when its ICD-10 underlying cause is X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (homicide) or Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent); a death enters a drug's count when that drug is mentioned in any of three certificate text fields (Part I causes, Part II contributing conditions, how the injury occurred), found by NCHS software (the Drugs Mentioned with Involvement, DMI, method) and assumed to be involved unless the surrounding words say otherwise. Deaths with several drugs are counted under each. Outputs: annual counts and percentages for the top 15 drugs (Table A), age-adjusted rates for 16 drugs with joinpoint trend tests (Table; Figures 1 to 4), the three commonest other drugs found with each of the top 10 drugs in 2023 (Table B), and the top 10 drugs by intent in 2023 (Table C). No toxicology data and no external validation. Filed as evidence-report with the editors' evidence-report checklist, as the round brief directs for statistics by public bodies.
can_establish: How many US drug overdose deaths in 2017 to 2023 (as defined by the four ICD-10 underlying-cause ranges) had each specific drug written on the death certificate, at minimum, how those counts and age-adjusted rates changed, which drugs were written together, and how the drugs named differed by recorded intent.
cannot_establish: How many deaths each drug caused (a mention is taken as involvement, and in multi-drug deaths the contribution of each drug cannot be told apart), how many deaths involving a drug were missed (the counts are minimums, toxicology practice is unseen and varies), how far trends reflect better reporting rather than real change (specificity rose from 87.7% to 96.0%), or anything about drug deaths outside these codes (chronic effects, adverse effects of therapeutic doses, deaths with other underlying causes).

sample.recruitment: Registry: all death certificates in the NVSS mortality files for 2017 to 2023 for US residents who died in the United States (NCHS codes data from 57 jurisdictions, mostly states), linked to literal text and retrieved on 6 April 2025 from a live database that continues to receive updates after the final files close, so counts may differ from other published sources (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Data and Methods › Data source and study population, 1st to 3rd paragraphs). n_total is the editors' sum of the seven annual totals in Table A.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: underlying cause X40 to X44, X60 to X64, X85 or Y10 to Y14, which reflect acute intoxication. Excluded: deaths from chronic exposure to drugs (such as liver toxicity), adverse effects of therapeutic or prophylactic doses, and deaths of non-residents or abroad (Data and Methods › Data source and study population, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Not reported in this report (no breakdown by sex, age or race). Manner across the period: unintentional 87% to 93%, suicide 4% to 7%, undetermined 3% to 5%, homicide 0.2% (Data source and study population, 1st paragraph). 2023: 98,497 unintentional, 4,711 suicide, 2,926 undetermined, 218 homicide (Table C; Results › by intent, 1st paragraph); these add to the 2023 total of 106,352 (editors' arithmetic).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Counts of 1 to 9 deaths are not shown and rates based on fewer than 20 deaths are not shown (Analysis, 3rd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: A death can enter a drug-specific count only if the certifier (usually a medical examiner or coroner for overdose deaths) wrote that drug on the certificate; whether toxicology was done, what was tested and how results were interpreted vary by jurisdiction, decedent and year (Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, bulleted list). Deaths without a named drug or drug class cannot enter any drug's count: 12.3% of overdose deaths in 2017 and 4.0% in 2023 had no ICD-10 multiple-cause code in T36.0 to T50.8 (about 8,700 and 4,300 deaths, editors' arithmetic from the percentages and annual totals). Drug deaths coded to other underlying causes are outside the overdose total by definition.

exposure.measurement: Drug involvement = a mention in the literal text written by the medical certifier, searched by the DMI software across Part I, Part II and the how-injury-occurred field (Introduction, 2nd paragraph). A mentioned drug is assumed involved unless contextual terms indicate otherwise (for example 'not drug related', or 'methicillin' within the name of an infection) (Identifying drug mentions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Search terms include generic and brand names, street names, abbreviations, metabolites and misspellings; the updated list was applied to the whole period, so numbers can differ from earlier reports (3rd paragraph). Terms map to 'principal variants' linked to the FDA's unique ingredient identifiers, and these to 'referent drug groups' defined with FDA and NCHS expertise; for example the fentanyl group includes analogues (carfentanil), precursors and metabolites (norfentanyl) (4th and 5th paragraphs). The full term and group list is in a supplementary spreadsheet, not read. NCHS sees no toxicology.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable; certificates record no amounts, and none are reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Every death is counted under every drug mentioned, so drug counts are not mutually exclusive: the top-15 counts sum to 1.47 times the total overdose deaths in 2017 and 1.69 times in 2023 (editors' arithmetic, Table A). Concomitant drugs were analysed for the top 10 drugs of 2023 (Table B); alcohol, nicotine and other non-drug substances were not included as concomitant substances (Analysis, 4th paragraph). The report states that for multi-drug deaths the text cannot show whether one drug or a combination caused the death (Discussion › Data considerations, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: No external comparison (no toxicology, enhanced surveillance or second register). Internal measure of reporting quality: the share of overdose deaths with at least one ICD-10 multiple-cause code in T36.0 to T50.8 (a drug or drug class named), 87.7% in 2017 to 96.0% in 2023. Comparisons are across years and across intent categories.

outcomes.instruments: Counts and percentages of overdose deaths with each referent drug mentioned; age-adjusted death rates (direct method, 2000 US standard population; 2010-based postcensal population estimates for 2017 to 2020 and the Census Bureau's July 1, 2024, estimate series on the blended base for 2021 to 2023); joinpoint regression (version 5.0.2, weighted least squares on log rates, up to two joinpoints, overall alpha 0.05); pairwise comparisons of rates between years by methods described elsewhere (Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: The DMI method is described in earlier NCHS reports; this report does not validate mentions against toxicology or case review.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Drug overdose death' = acute intoxication as underlying cause (the four ICD-10 ranges). 'Involving' a drug = the drug mentioned anywhere in the three text fields, including Part II, unless context negates it. 'Concomitant drug' = another specific drug mentioned on the same certificate.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across drugs: 16 drug-specific joinpoint trend analyses (Table), each with its own overall alpha of 0.05 for model selection, plus pairwise year comparisons whose number is not stated. Ranks were not tested for significance (Tables A and C, footnote 1).

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts, percentages, age-adjusted rates per 100,000 standard population and annual percent changes; no intervals. Totals: 70,715 (2017) to 108,790 (2022), up 53.8%, then 106,352 (2023); up 50.4% from 2017 to 2023 (both checked, editors' arithmetic). Fentanyl: 27,542 deaths (38.9%) in 2017 to 73,944 in 2022 and 73,297 (68.9%) in 2023; rate 8.8 (2017), 21.8 (2021, about 29% a year), 22.7 (2022), 22.3 (2023). Methamphetamine: 9,438 (13.3%) to 34,167 (32.1%); rate 3.0 to 9.7 (2021, about 37% a year), then 10.4 (2023, stable). Cocaine: 15,050 (21.3%) to 31,700 (29.8%); rate 4.7 to 9.3, about 14% a year. Heroin: 16,085 (22.7%) to 4,071 (3.8%); rate 5.1 to 1.2, falling about 6% a year in 2017 to 2020 and about 35% a year in 2020 to 2023. Xylazine: 12 deaths (2017; rate not shown) and 102 (2018, rate 0.0) to 6,096 (5.7%, rate 1.9) in 2023, about 61% a year from 2018. Oxycodone rate 1.9 to 1.2 (down 36.8%, trend not significant); morphine 1.5 to 0.7 (significant fall from 2021); methadone, hydrocodone, clonazepam, diazepam and alprazolam without significant trend; gabapentin 0.6 to 1.3 (2021, about 27% a year), then stable at 1.2; amphetamine 0.5 to 1.3 (2021, about 28% a year); bromazolam 151 deaths (0.1) in 2021 to 1,734 (0.5) in 2023 (Results; Table A; Table). All Table A percentages reproduce from their counts and annual totals, and the counts agree between Table A and the rates table (editors' check of all 105 Table A cells).
analysis.covariates: Age adjustment only; no breakdown or adjustment by sex, race, region or jurisdiction.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Routine statistical report; methods follow earlier NCHS reports in the series.
analysis.selective_reporting: The report gives the share of deaths with a T36.0 to T50.8 code (drug or drug class) but never the number with at least one specific drug identified by the DMI search, although its abstract and Table A describe results among deaths with at least one specific drug mentioned. No results by jurisdiction are given, although the Discussion names jurisdictional variation in investigation and certification as a main limitation. The rate denominators change from 2010-based postcensal estimates (2017 to 2020) to the July 1, 2024, blended-base series (2021 to 2023) without comment on the trend analyses.
analysis.power: Not applicable (national census of registered deaths); small counts are suppressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US overdose deaths defined by ICD-10 underlying cause, the drugs most often written on certificates in 2017 to 2023 were fentanyl (first every year; 68.9% of overdose deaths in 2023), methamphetamine and cocaine; heroin mentions fell steeply; xylazine, gabapentin and bromazolam rose; fentanyl was written with most other top drugs (99.0% of xylazine deaths, 48.3% of oxycodone deaths); and the drugs named differed by intent (fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine in unintentional deaths; diphenhydramine, oxycodone and bupropion in suicides). All counts are minimums of deaths with a drug mentioned, and naming of drugs became more complete over the period.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report keeps to 'involved' and 'mentioned', states that counts are minimums and that the text cannot show which drug caused a multi-drug death, and warns that better reporting may explain part of some increases (Discussion › Data considerations, 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs). Gaps: (1) the fentanyl rate change from 2022 to 2023 is described as stabilising (Abstract), as a decrease to 22.3 (Results), and as a decrease that was not statistically significant (Discussion › Findings, 3rd paragraph), while the Table and Figure 2 footnotes say the 2023 rate was lower than the 2022 rate at p<0.05; (2) the Discussion says the fentanyl rate almost tripled from 2017 to 2021, while the Table gives 8.8 to 21.8, about 2.5 times (editors' arithmetic); (3) the Discussion says oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, clonazepam and diazepam had little to no decreases, while the oxycodone rate fell 36.8% by the report's own figure and hydrocodone from 0.9 to 0.6: these trends were not statistically significant, which is not the same as small; (4) the improvement from 87.7% to 96.0% is described in the Discussion and in the notes to the rates table and Figures 1 to 4 as reporting of at least one specific drug in the literal text, while the Methods and Table A define it as a T36.0 to T50.8 code, which can be a drug class; (5) the Discussion attributes the fall in overdose suicides from 5,086 (2016) to 4,711 (2023) to opioid-class drugs using a 2016 figure from the previous report, whose search-term list differs, although the report warns that numbers may differ from earlier reports for that reason; (6) the Discussion lists methamphetamine among drugs with steep increases between 2017 and 2023, while the Results and the Table's footnote give a significant rise only from 2017 to 2021 (3.0 to 9.7) and call the rate stable from 2021 (9.7) to 2023 (10.4).

timeline.event: Trinidad et al., NCHS: the literal-text method for characterising drug involvement in deaths (National Vital Statistics Reports 65(9); ref 7; listed as report R4 on the project's drug-deaths list).
Warner et al., NCHS: drugs most frequently involved in overdose deaths, 2010 to 2014 (ref 21; report R5 on the project's list).
Hedegaard et al., NCHS: the same analysis for 2011 to 2016, which this report updates (ref 10).
This report: 2017 to 2023, with an expanded search-term list applied to the whole period.

replication.where_it_stands: The current national NCHS series turning certificate text into drug-specific counts. Its counts are minimums of deaths with a drug written on the certificate, not of deaths caused by it, and their completeness depends on toxicology and certification practices that NCHS does not see. Studies on this project's drug-deaths list measure that gap from outside the certificate (for example Slavova et al., 2015, on state variation in naming the drug; Buchanich et al., 2018, on incomplete certificates; Horon et al., 2018, comparing certificates with enhanced surveillance); claims about how much drug-specific counts are understated should cite them, not this report.

funding.funder: Not reported. The report is a National Center for Health Statistics publication (National Vital Statistics Reports); no funding statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors' affiliations are not printed beside their names; the report's back matter lists NCHS and its Divisions of Vital Statistics and of Analysis and Epidemiology, and the acknowledgements thank NCHS reviewers and Information Technology Branch staff (two of them contractors) who ran the DMI processing. Margaret Warner and Bruce Goldberger are thanked for expertise and guidance; Goldberger, a forensic toxicologist, co-chaired the 2013 SAMHSA consensus panel on definitions (card sc_goldberger_2013). No commercial interest is apparent.

what_would_settle_it: Link a national sample of overdose death certificates, including those naming no drug, to their full toxicology reports and investigation files, and measure by jurisdiction, year and drug how often a drug found and judged contributory is missing from the certificate text, how often a mentioned drug was incidental, and how often heroin is recorded as morphine; repeating this over time would separate real trends from improvements in reporting.

domains.note: For a statistics report this concerns case ascertainment: every registered death of a US resident in the United States with one of the four stated ICD-10 underlying-cause ranges, with exclusions and the data extraction date stated. The definition itself leaves out drug deaths coded to other underlying causes, which the report states.

Read as appraisal of the data source: the report measures the specificity of drug reporting each year and lists the limitations of certificate text (toxicology practice, interpretation, metabolites, choice of drugs to list, software space limits), but does not validate mentions against toxicology or case review, gives no jurisdiction-level quality measures and cannot separate causal from co-present drugs.

Read as stated rules for counting and reporting: the ICD-10 codes, the DMI rules (mention means involvement unless context negates; term mapping and referent groups), multiple counting, the joinpoint settings and the suppression thresholds are all stated; the full term list is in a supplement. The reliability threshold is worded both as 20 or more and as more than 20 deaths.
A federal statistical agency's routine report by its own staff; no funding or interests statement is printed, and no commercial interest is apparent.
Review by named NCHS staff in other divisions and the Office of the Director, and data-file quality checks by the Division of Vital Statistics; no external peer review is described.

The Conclusions are descriptive and the caveats (minimum counts, improved reporting, no attribution within multi-drug deaths) are clear, but the Discussion contradicts the Table and Figure 2 on the significance of the 2022 to 2023 fentanyl fall, overstates the 2017 to 2021 fentanyl rise, calls non-significant falls of about a third 'little to no decreases', describes a drug-or-class code measure as specific-drug reporting, compares 2023 suicides with a 2016 figure built with a different term list, and lists methamphetamine among steep increases from 2017 to 2023 although its rate was stable from 2021.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Filed as design evidence-report with the editors' evidence-report checklist, as the round brief directs for statistics by public bodies; the six domains are read for a statistics report rather than an evidence synthesis (case ascertainment for search and selection; appraisal of the data source; stated counting rules). As a count of what US certificates say, the report is complete, transparent and internally consistent in its tables (every Table A percentage and the counts shared between tables reproduce). Its limits are those of certificate text, which it states plainly, and a handful of discussion statements that go beyond or against its own tables. It may be cited, attributed to NCHS, for the ICD-10 definition of overdose deaths used in US statistics, for how drug-specific counts are built from certificate text (mention taken as involvement; multi-drug deaths counted under each drug), for the minimum numbers and rates of deaths with each drug mentioned, for the concomitant-drug percentages and for the drugs named by intent, and for the growth in drug-specific reporting from 87.7% to 96.0%. It may not be cited for deaths caused by a drug, for the size of any undercount, for the significance of the 2022 to 2023 fentanyl change without noting the report's conflicting statements, or as showing that the drugs listed with fentanyl contributed to the deaths.

key_findings.finding: Overdose deaths were defined by ICD-10 underlying cause X40 to X44 (unintentional), X60 to X64 (suicide), X85 (homicide) and Y10 to Y14 (undetermined intent), which reflect acute intoxication; deaths from chronic drug exposure (such as liver toxicity) and adverse effects of therapeutic or prophylactic doses were excluded; only US residents who died in the United States were included. Across 2017 to 2023 the manner was unintentional in 87% to 93% of these deaths, suicide 4% to 7%, undetermined 3% to 5%, homicide 0.2%.
key_findings.locator: Data and Methods › Data source and study population, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: In 2023 the undetermined share was 2,926 of 106,352, 2.75% (editors' arithmetic), within the stated 3% to 5% only after rounding.

key_findings.finding: Why certificate text is searched: ICD-10 drug codes are broad. Fentanyl, Demerol, tramadol, nitazenes and Suboxone all fall under T40.4 ('other synthetic narcotics', usually published as synthetic opioids other than methadone), and oxycodone falls under T40.2 ('other opioids') with drugs such as codeine and morphine, so code-based data cannot track specific drugs.

The literal text is written by the medical certifier, usually a medical examiner or coroner for overdose deaths; NCHS searches three fields of the US standard certificate: Part I causes, Part II significant contributing conditions, and how the injury occurred.

Counting rule: a drug mentioned in the text is assumed to be involved in the death unless contextual words indicate otherwise (for example 'not drug related'). Search terms cover generic and brand names, street names, abbreviations, metabolites and misspellings, mapped to principal variants (linked to FDA unique ingredient identifiers) and grouped into referent drug groups chosen with FDA and NCHS expertise; the fentanyl group includes fentanyl analogues such as carfentanil, precursors and metabolites such as norfentanyl. The updated term list was applied to all years, so numbers can differ from earlier reports.
key_findings.locator: Data and Methods › Identifying drug mentions and involvement of the drug in the death, 1st to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Deaths involving more than one drug are counted in every relevant drug's count, percentage and rate (a death with cocaine and heroin is in both). In consequence the 15 drug-specific counts in Table A sum to 103,675 against 70,715 deaths in 2017 (1.47 times) and 179,965 against 106,352 in 2023 (1.69 times).
key_findings.note: Sums and ratios are editors' arithmetic from Table A.

key_findings.finding: NCHS states that the drug-specific numbers and rates may be undercounts and should be read as minimums, because a drug may have been involved without being written on the certificate.
key_findings.locator: Analysis, 5th paragraph; Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Specificity of drug reporting: the share of overdose deaths with at least one ICD-10 multiple-cause code in T36.0 to T50.8 rose every year: 87.7% (2017), 92.0%, 93.8%, 94.4%, 95.2%, 95.8%, 96.0% (2023). NCHS says this improvement could influence the observed trends, that some increases may be partly due to better reporting but large increases are unlikely to be explained by it alone, and that better reporting could obscure real declines.
key_findings.locator: Data and Methods › Measuring the percentage of specific drugs on death certificates; Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sources of error named by NCHS, in both directions: whether toxicology is done and what is tested vary by jurisdiction, decedent and year; interpretation depends on the tests ordered and the investigation; shared metabolites can misattribute drugs (morphine mentions may reflect heroin, underestimating heroin and overestimating morphine); some certifiers list a single lethal drug while others list several, and some say electronic registration software limits the space for drugs; rarely mentioned drugs may be missing from the term list.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 3rd paragraph, bulleted list and 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: For multi-drug deaths, the literal-text analysis cannot determine whether one drug or a combination caused the death.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Data considerations and study limitations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Overdose deaths rose from 70,715 in 2017 to 108,790 in 2022 (53.8%) and were 106,352 in 2023. Fentanyl ranked first every year: 27,542 deaths (38.9%) in 2017, 73,944 in 2022, 73,297 (68.9%) in 2023. Methamphetamine rose from 9,438 (13.3%) to 34,167 (32.1%), from fourth to second; cocaine from 15,050 (21.3%) to 31,700 (29.8%); heroin fell from 16,085 (22.7%, second) to 4,071 (3.8%, seventh); xylazine entered the top 15 in 2021 (3,501) and was fourth in 2023 (6,096, 5.7%); bromazolam entered in 2023 (1,734, 1.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Most frequently mentioned drugs, bulleted list; Table A

key_findings.finding: Age-adjusted rates per 100,000: fentanyl 8.8 (2017) to 21.8 (2021), about 29% a year, then 22.7 (2022) and 22.3 (2023); heroin 5.1 to 1.2, falling about 6% a year in 2017 to 2020 and about 35% a year in 2020 to 2023; methamphetamine 3.0 to 9.7 (2021, about 37% a year), then 10.4; cocaine 4.7 to 9.3 (about 14% a year); xylazine 0.0 (2018) to 1.9 (about 61% a year); oxycodone 1.9 to 1.2 (down 36.8%, not significant); morphine 1.5 to 0.7 (significant fall from 2021).
key_findings.locator: Results › Age-adjusted rates, Selected opioids, Fentanyl and xylazine and Selected stimulants bullets; Table, with footnotes 1 to 8
key_findings.note: Table footnote 4 and the Figure 2 legend say the 2023 fentanyl rate was lower than the 2022 rate at p<0.05; the Discussion says this fall was not significant (reporting issue 1).

key_findings.finding: Drugs written together in 2023 (Table B): fentanyl was the commonest other drug for 9 of the top 10 drugs, from 99.0% of xylazine deaths (6,033 of 6,096) and 81.9% of heroin deaths to 57.4% of methadone and 48.3% of oxycodone deaths (2,002 of 4,142), and 76.0% of cocaine and 66.5% of methamphetamine deaths. Among fentanyl deaths, cocaine was written in 32.9%, methamphetamine 31.0% and xylazine 8.2%. Alcohol, nicotine and non-drug substances were not counted as concomitant drugs.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug overdose deaths in 2023 involving multiple drugs, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table B; Analysis, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Drugs by intent in 2023 (Table C): unintentional deaths (98,497) most often mentioned fentanyl 71.9%, methamphetamine 33.9% and cocaine 31.0%; suicides (4,711) diphenhydramine 14.7%, oxycodone 10.3%, bupropion 9.8%, fentanyl 9.7%, acetaminophen 8.0%; undetermined-intent deaths (2,926) fentanyl 63.2%, cocaine 32.5%, methamphetamine 13.9%. The 218 homicides are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most frequently mentioned drugs ... by intent of death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table C

key_findings.finding: Overdose suicides fell from 5,086 in 2016 to 4,711 in 2023 while the overall suicide rate rose; NCHS attributes the fall to fewer opioid-class mentions, including oxycodone 648 (12.7%) to 485 (10.3%) and hydrocodone 472 (9.3%) to 315 (6.7%), with morphine leaving the top 10.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: The 2016 figures come from the previous report (ref 10), built with an older search-term list (reporting issue 5).

reporting_issues.issue: The fentanyl rate change from 2022 (22.7) to 2023 (22.3) is described in three ways: stabilised (Abstract), decreased (Results), and decreased but not statistically significant (Discussion › Findings, 3rd paragraph); the Table footnote 4 and the Figure 2 legend state that the 2023 rate was lower than the 2022 rate at p<0.05.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Abstract; Results › Fentanyl and xylazine; Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Table, footnote 4; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether fentanyl-involved deaths fell significantly in 2023 cannot be settled from the report; claims should give the rates and note the conflict.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the fentanyl rate almost tripled between 2017 and 2021; the Table gives 8.8 and 21.8, a ratio of about 2.5 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Table
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the rates, not the description.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists oxycodone, hydrocodone, methadone, clonazepam and diazepam as having little to no decreases, while the Results give a 36.8% fall in the oxycodone rate (1.9 to 1.2) and the Table shows hydrocodone 0.9 to 0.6 and diazepam 0.7 to 0.5; these trends were not statistically significant.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Results › Selected opioids; Table
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-significant trend should not be cited as no change.

reporting_issues.issue: The specificity measure is defined in the Methods and the Table A note as at least one ICD-10 code in T36.0 to T50.8 (a drug or drug class), but the Discussion and the notes to the rates table and Figures 1 to 4 describe the same 88% to 96% as reporting of at least one specific drug in the literal text. The number of deaths with at least one specific drug found by the DMI search is never given, although the Abstract and Table A describe their results among such deaths.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Data and Methods › Measuring the percentage of specific drugs; Table A note; Table note; Discussion › Data considerations, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 96.0% is a drug-or-class figure; the share of overdose deaths with no specific drug named may be larger than 4.0%.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion compares overdose suicides in 2023 (4,711) with 2016 (5,086) and the opioid figures of 2016 from the previous report, although the report says its updated term list makes numbers differ from earlier reports, and attributes the fall to opioid-class drugs although deaths can count under several drugs.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 5th paragraph; Identifying drug mentions, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2016 to 2023 comparison is not on a consistent method; cite it as approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The notes to Tables B and C say only deaths with at least one specific drug identified were analysed, but the Table C denominators (98,497, 4,711, 2,926, with 218 homicides) add to all 106,352 overdose deaths of 2023; and the Analysis says the concomitant analysis includes only deaths with at least two specific drugs, while Table B's percentages use all deaths with the referent drug as denominators.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Table B note; Table C note and column headings; Analysis, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentages in Tables B and C are of all overdose deaths in the category (or with the referent drug), as the arithmetic confirms; the notes describe the inclusion rule loosely.

reporting_issues.issue: The reliability threshold is given as fewer than 20 deaths (Analysis; Table), as 20 or more (Figure 2 legend) and as more than 20 (Figure 3 legend); the Figure 3 legend says bromazolam rates for 2017 to 2020 do not meet it, while the Table shows no data for 2017 to 2019 and a suppressed count of fewer than 10 for 2020, and the text says bromazolam first appeared in 2020.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Analysis, 3rd paragraph; Table footnotes; Figure 2 and Figure 3 legends; Results › Selected benzodiazepines and anticonvulsants
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no effect on the published rates.

reporting_issues.issue: Population denominators change from 2010-based postcensal estimates (2017 to 2020) to the July 1, 2024, blended-base series (2021 to 2023) inside the trend series, without comment on the joinpoint results.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably small, but a break in the denominator falls at the point where several trends change slope (2020 to 2021).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists methamphetamine among drugs with steep increases between 2017 and 2023, while the Results say its rate rose from 3.0 to 9.7 between 2017 and 2021 and was stable from 2021 (9.7) to 2023 (10.4), and the Table's footnote 6 gives a significant increasing trend for 2017 to 2021 only. The trend periods also differ for cocaine: the Table's footnote 8 and the Results give a significant increase from 2017 to 2023 (about 14% a year), while the Figure 4 legend marks the cocaine line with a significant increasing trend from 2021 to 2023.
reporting_issues.page: Bookshelf HTML, Discussion › Findings for specific drugs, 3rd paragraph; Results › Selected stimulants; Table, footnotes 6 and 8; Figure 4 and its legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite methamphetamine as rising from 2017 to 2021 with a stable rate to 2023, and take trend periods from the Table's footnotes, not from the Discussion or the Figure 4 legend.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results call methamphetamine, and then cocaine, the second or third most frequent concomitant drug among the other top drugs; by Table B, methamphetamine is not among the three for oxycodone (alprazolam 19.1% and cocaine 17.2% are second and third), and cocaine is the most frequent, not the second or third, for fentanyl (32.9%).
